passage: So you want to know about the chips thing? Okay. I'm Divyansh, and during board prep last March I studied from six in the morning till almost nine at night. By evening my brain was porridge. My sister Lakshmi would ask, "Dal or khichdi for dinner?" and I'd just say "whatever." Then I'd open the cupboard and eat a whole packet of masala chips standing up. Friends texted me real questions, like whether to join the group revision on Sunday, and I'd send a thumbs-up without reading properly. Twice I agreed to things I didn't want. Lakshmi finally noticed and started asking me the big stuff at breakfast, when I could still think. Honestly, that helped more than any timetable.

qa.q: What did Divyansh eat standing up in the evenings?
qa.a: Divyansh ate a whole packet of masala chips standing up.

qa.q: Why did saying "whatever" and sending a thumbs-up feel reasonable to Divyansh at night?
qa.a: After studying from six till nine Divyansh felt drained and foggy, so any choice felt like one too many and the easiest option brought relief.

qa.q: What small change could protect Divyansh's choices during exam weeks?
qa.a: Keep real questions for the morning, as Lakshmi began doing, and decide simple dinner and snack options earlier in the day so evening choices are already made.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt when Divyansh kept answering "whatever"?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt brushed off at first, then worried, which is why Lakshmi moved the big questions to breakfast.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after long study hours, grabs junk snacks and gives quick replies because choosing has worn them out.

passage:
Monday. Aditi finished her physics mock at noon, planned the whole week's revision, picked which chapters to redo, chose a new pen colour for each subject and felt oddly powerful.

Wednesday. After three more hours of past papers, her cousin Tanuja asked which film they should watch on Saturday. Aditi stared at the list, said "you pick," then ordered a sugary cold coffee she didn't even like and snapped at the delivery man for being late.

Friday. Aditi tried something Tanuja suggested: she wrote tomorrow's lunch, study order and one fun thing on a sticky note before breakfast. That evening she followed the note without arguing with herself and slept earlier than she had all week.

qa.q: What did Aditi write on the sticky note on Friday?
qa.a: She wrote tomorrow's lunch, study order and one fun thing.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on Wednesday when she said "you pick" and snapped at the delivery man?
qa.a: She was worn out and irritable after hours of past papers, so even choosing a film felt like a burden and she grabbed the quickest option.

qa.q: Which choice worked on Friday, and why?
qa.a: Deciding small things in the morning worked because Aditi used her fresh energy for them and did not have to choose again when she was tired.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the change in Aditi between Wednesday and Friday?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt snubbed on Wednesday and then glad on Friday to see Aditi calmer and easier to be around.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after many choices on exam days, falls back on quick, easy options until planning small decisions ahead helps.

passage: Sit, Sarita, and let your Ama Dolma tell you something before your exams. When I was a girl of sixteen in Darjeeling, we had the school leaving exams in winter. I studied by the stove from dawn, choosing which chapter, which notes, which question to try first. By evening I could not decide anything. My mother would ask, "Tea with salt or sugar?" and I would just take whatever was nearest. One night I bought three packets of sweets from the corner shop with my bus money and walked home in the cold. My teacher saw me yawning and said, "Make your hard choices before lunch, Dolma." So I did. The evenings became simple: same meal, same walk, bed. My marks were not perfect, but my head was clearer.

qa.q: What did Dolma buy with the bus money one night?
qa.a: Dolma bought three packets of sweets from the corner shop.

qa.q: Why did buying the sweets feel reasonable to young Dolma at the time?
qa.a: After a whole day of choosing chapters and questions Dolma felt exhausted, and the sweets were an easy comfort that needed no thinking.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Dolma's evenings?
qa.a: Dolma's teacher told her to make hard choices before lunch, and after that Dolma kept her evenings simple with the same meal, walk and bedtime.

qa.q: How might Dolma's mother have seen her daughter during those exam weeks?
qa.a: Dolma's mother may have been puzzled and a little concerned that Dolma could not even pick salt or sugar in her tea.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenager in exam season, hours of choosing left her grabbing easy sweets and not deciding.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Block C, Thursday.

I have been watching Charu, a second-year student, at the mess counter this week. Mornings she is organised: she chooses her classes, argues sensibly about a project plan with her roommate Nirmala, even decides the weekend travel. By eight at night she stands at the counter for a long time, then takes only a sweet bun, skips the dal and goes upstairs. Twice she told Nirmala she would answer the project email "later" and did not.

Today I asked her how the day had gone. She laughed and said, "Too many choices, ma'am, I'm out of choosing." I suggested she fix her dinner and one evening task before lunch. She wrote them in her phone. I will check in next week.

qa.a: Charu feels drained and weary from a day of choosing classes, plans and travel, and the bun and "later" spare her one more decision.

qa.a: The warden suggested fixing dinner and one evening task before lunch, so Charu makes those choices while her mind is still fresh.

qa.a: Nirmala is left waiting on the project email and may feel frustrated or unsure whether Charu cares about their shared work.

"It's ten in the morning, Rajni. Perfect time. Let's go through it now."

"What if they push for an answer at six?"

"Then I'll say we'll reply by ten tomorrow. I don't sign things when I'm hungry or tired."

passage:
Last year I nearly accepted a transfer to Pune at 11 p.m. after a fourteen-hour shift. My manager Samir had messaged, "Need your answer tonight if possible." I typed "yes" and then, for some reason, didn't press send.

In the morning, after chai and a proper breakfast, I read the offer again. The pay looked fine, but the role would have kept me travelling every week, and my mother's check-ups were in Mumbai. I called Samir at nine and asked for two days.

Since then I have a rule for myself. Big choices happen between nine and noon. My clothes, my breakfast and my commute are fixed, so I don't waste thinking on them. If I'm starving or rushed, I say, "Let me come back to you." I'm Manoj, and I've learnt that tired Manoj agrees to everything.

qa.q: At what time did Manoj nearly accept the transfer to Pune?
qa.a: Manoj nearly accepted it at 11 p.m. after a fourteen-hour shift.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel reading the offer again in the morning?
qa.a: Manoj felt steadier and clearer, and probably relieved about not pressing send, because the weekly travel and the mother's check-ups in Mumbai were now plain to see.

qa.q: What routine helps Manoj save thinking for big decisions?
qa.a: Manoj fixes clothes, breakfast and commute, and keeps big choices for nine to noon.

qa.q: How might Samir have seen Manoj's request for two more days?
qa.a: Samir may have been slightly impatient but also reassured that Manoj was taking the move seriously rather than saying yes carelessly.

grounding: A young professional learns to make big decisions early, use routines for small ones and avoid choices when worn out.

The notice on the school board said: Inter-school Science Fair, entries close Friday. Neelam read it three times during lunch.

"Your water filter idea would win something," said Simran, holding out the form.

"Or it'd fall apart in front of judges from six schools."

"So?"

Neelam folded the form into a tiny square. "If I don't enter, nobody can say it was bad."

In chemistry lab, she kept glancing at her old sketch in the back of her notebook. On Thursday evening she almost filled the form, then put it back in her bag.

On Saturday Simran messaged her a photo of the prize table. Neelam looked at it for a long time and didn't reply.

qa.q: What did the notice on the school board say?
qa.a: It said Inter-school Science Fair, entries close Friday.

qa.q: Why did skipping the fair feel safer to Neelam?
qa.a: Neelam was afraid of the embarrassment and regret of failing in front of judges, and not entering felt like protection.

qa.q: What small step could help Neelam next time an entry form comes up?
qa.a: She could fill it in with Simran right away, before fear builds, and remind herself that not trying also leaves a regret.

qa.q: How might Simran feel when Neelam doesn't reply to the photo?
qa.a: Simran might feel sad for her friend and unsure whether sending the photo helped or hurt.

grounding: A teenager avoids entering a competition, fearing the regret of failing more than the regret of never trying.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,

You asked if I'd told Harleen how I feel. I didn't. I had it all planned for the school trip on Saturday. I'd even practised what to say. Then on the bus I kept picturing her face going blank and everyone finding out. I thought, if she says no, I'll regret it forever. So I talked about the museum instead.

Now it's Tuesday and she's been sitting with someone else at lunch. I keep telling myself that at least I didn't get rejected. But it doesn't feel like a win. It feels like I left a question open that will never close.

Next time, I think I'd rather hear no than hear nothing.

Write back soon,
Gurpreet

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet plan to talk to Harleen?
qa.a: Gurpreet planned to talk to Harleen on the school trip on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet afraid of on the bus?
qa.a: Gurpreet was scared of Harleen saying no and feared the lasting regret and embarrassment of rejection.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet try when a similar chance comes up again?
qa.a: Gurpreet could say the simple words early, before the what-ifs grow, and accept that a clear no is easier to live with than never knowing.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Elizabeth might feel sympathy for Gurpreet and want to encourage trying next time, since the regret of not asking is clear in the letter.

grounding: A teenager avoids asking someone out, fearing the regret of rejection more than the regret of never trying, and feels that second regret later.

passage:
Can I tell you something embarrassing? I'm Aadhya, and in class ten there was this state-level debate competition. My English teacher said I should apply. My best friend Preeti even printed the form for me.

I kept it in my maths book for two weeks. Every time I thought about it, I pictured myself forgetting my points on stage. Then I'd feel better if I just... didn't. I told myself not trying was the smart option. No failure, no regret.

The deadline passed. Preeti went instead, and she came third. I clapped for her, I really did. But on the bus home I was quiet. I kept thinking, that could have been my third place, or even my last place, and at least I'd know.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya keep the debate form for two weeks?
qa.a: Aadhya kept the form in a maths book for two weeks.

qa.q: Why did not applying feel like "the smart option" to Aadhya?
qa.a: Picturing forgetting points on stage made Aadhya anxious, and skipping felt like relief from the risk of failure and regret.

qa.q: What would you advise Aadhya to do with the next competition form?
qa.a: Submit it soon, maybe with Preeti's help, and remember that even a last place teaches more than never knowing.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt coming third while her friend stayed home?
qa.a: Preeti may have felt proud of her result but also a little sad that Aadhya wasn't there with her.

grounding: A teenager avoids applying for a competition, fearing the regret of failing more than never trying, and later feels the regret of inaction.

passage:
Dear Rashmi,

Thanks for asking about the offer. I took the bank job. Mummy was relieved and Papa told everyone at the wedding last week that his son is a banker now.

You know I'd been planning the film course for two years. But every time I imagined it not working, I heard people saying, "Sahil threw away a good job for a hobby." I couldn't stand the idea of being the one who made the wrong call. The bank felt like nobody could blame me.

It's been a month. The work is fine. I'm good at it. But on the metro home I still watch short films on my phone and feel a pang I can't explain to anyone.

Is it strange that I chose the safe thing and still feel like I'm going to regret it?

Sahil

qa.q: Which job did Sahil take?
qa.a: Sahil took the bank job.

qa.q: Why did the bank job feel safer to Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil was afraid of the regret and blame of failing at the film course and felt nobody could criticise the bank job.

qa.q: What could Sahil do now to keep the film interest alive?
qa.a: Sahil could take a short evening or weekend film class, or talk with a trusted person about a longer-term plan, instead of just watching on the metro.

qa.q: How might Rashmi respond to Sahil's question?
qa.a: Rashmi might reassure Sahil that the feeling is not strange and that playing safe can bring its own regret.

grounding: A young adult picks a safe job to avoid blame for a mistake, only to feel the regret of the path not taken.

I'm Kiran, and people always ask me why I did commerce when I was mad about architecture. Here's the honest version. In class twelve my friend Nilesh and I both wanted to apply for design school. The entrance exam was hard and you had to make a portfolio. I kept thinking, if I apply and don't get in, I've wasted a year and everyone will know.

Commerce was the safe stream. Nobody questions you. So I filled the commerce form, and Nilesh applied to design.

He got in. I passed commerce fine. Four years later, I help plan buildings' budgets and sometimes stand in the office looking at the drawings. I didn't avoid regret at all, I just picked a slower kind of it.

qa.q: Which stream did Kiran choose?
qa.a: Kiran chose commerce, the safe stream.

qa.a: Kiran was afraid of failing, wasting a year and feeling the shame of everyone knowing.

qa.q: What could someone in Kiran's place try before choosing the safe path?
qa.a: They could ask themselves how they would feel years later about not trying, and talk it through with a teacher or counsellor before deciding.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Kiran's choice now?
qa.a: Nilesh might feel sad that Kiran never tried, since they had both wanted design and he knows how much Kiran loved it.

grounding: A young adult chooses the safe stream to avoid being seen to fail, and later feels the regret of inaction.

passage:
July. Wasim received two offers: a government clerk post in his hometown and a junior role at a small startup in Bengaluru. He wanted the startup. But he pictured it folding and his uncles saying, "We told you so." He accepted the government post the same week.

October. His friend Gopika sent him photos from the startup's first product launch. She had joined the role he had turned down. Wasim liked the photos, then turned his phone face down on his desk.

January. At dinner, he told Gopika over a video call, "I thought taking the safe job meant I couldn't regret anything. I was wrong." She suggested he look at part-time projects while he figured it out. He opened a notebook and wrote a list.

qa.q: What were Wasim's two offers?
qa.a: A government clerk post in his hometown and a junior role at a small startup in Bengaluru.

qa.q: How was Wasim feeling when he turned his phone face down in October?
qa.a: He felt a pang of regret and maybe jealousy seeing the launch photos from the job he had turned down.

qa.q: What small step did Wasim take in January, and why might it help?
qa.a: He wrote a list of part-time projects, which lets him explore his interest without making another all-or-nothing choice.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Wasim's decision?
qa.a: Gopika probably understands his fear but can see he is unhappy, so she tries to encourage him gently.

grounding: A young adult picks the safe job so nobody can say he made a mistake, and feels the regret of inaction months later.

passage:
March. Tejas had two job offers, one in Pune and one in Singapore, and a half-promise from his current firm about a promotion. He asked both companies for more time. His partner Maria asked if they should sign the new flat lease. "Let's wait until I know," he said.

May. The Pune offer was withdrawn. Singapore gave him a final week. The flat Maria liked had been rented to someone else. Tejas lay awake listing what-ifs.

June. Maria sat him down. "Waiting isn't free, Tejas. We lost the flat and one offer already." He wrote the two things that mattered most, family close and a team he trusted. Pune had been the answer. He told his firm he would stay one more year, and they signed a smaller flat that weekend.

qa.q: What happened to the Pune offer by May?
qa.a: The Pune offer was withdrawn.

qa.q: Why did Tejas keep asking for more time?
qa.a: He feared regretting whichever road he didn't take, so delaying felt safer and less frightening than committing.

qa.q: What helped Tejas finally decide in June?
qa.a: Maria pointed out the cost of waiting, and he wrote the two things that mattered most, which made his priorities clear.

qa.q: How does Maria experience Tejas's delays?
qa.a: Maria is frustrated and let down, since she loses the flat she liked while waiting for him to commit.

grounding: A young professional keeps every door open and delays commitment, and the delay costs him an offer and a home.

passage:
Mridul, beta, you're asking whether to accept this offer or wait for something better. Let me tell you about your Kamal chacha at your age.

At twenty-five I had a teaching post in Lucknow and an invitation to join a friend's printing business. I also dreamt of the civil services. I didn't want to close any door, so I kept all three going. I taught half-heartedly, promised my friend I'd join "after the exam," and studied late at night.

A year passed. My friend found another partner. The school gave my permanent post to someone who was fully there. And I failed the exam by a few marks, tired from juggling. The day I finally chose teaching properly, I felt lighter. But I'd lost a year, and a friend's trust.

qa.q: What three paths was Kamal keeping open at twenty-five?
qa.a: A teaching post in Lucknow, joining a friend's printing business, and the civil services.

qa.q: Why did Kamal try to keep all three paths going?
qa.a: Kamal was afraid of regretting whichever door got closed, so juggling everything felt safer than choosing.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for Kamal?
qa.a: After losing the partnership, the permanent post and the exam, Kamal finally chose teaching properly and felt lighter.

qa.q: How might Kamal's friend have felt when Kamal kept saying "after the exam"?
qa.a: The friend probably felt let down and unsure of Kamal, which is why the friend found another partner.

grounding: An elder recalls how keeping every door open and delaying commitment cost Kamal a job, a partnership and a year.

Anand had to answer Noor by midnight. She was a friend from college who had built a small bakery and wanted him as a partner before a big festival order. It was raining hard, the power was out in his building and his phone was on nine percent.

Anand had been saying "let me think" for three weeks. He still had a job interview pending in Dubai. What if the bakery failed? What if the Dubai job was the real chance?

At 11:40 his phone died. He sat in the dark and didn't borrow a neighbour's charger.

In the morning, Noor's message was waiting: "I've asked Farida to join instead. I needed someone who could say yes." Anand read it twice. The Dubai interviewers never called back.

qa.q: By what time did Anand have to answer Noor?
qa.a: He had to answer Noor by midnight.

qa.q: Why did Anand keep saying "let me think" for three weeks?
qa.a: He felt torn and afraid of regretting the road not taken, so delaying felt safer than committing to either the bakery or Dubai.

qa.q: What could Anand have done differently before the deadline?
qa.a: He could have listed what mattered most to him and given Noor a clear answer earlier, or at least asked for an exact extra day.

qa.q: How does Noor seem to see Anand's delay?
qa.a: Noor seems let down but practical; she needed someone who could commit and moved on to Farida.

grounding: A young professional delays commitment out of fear of regret, and the delay loses him both chances.
